name: Bastia-Poretta International airport
before:
The airport for Bastia and the north of Corsica, 17 km south south east of the city at Lucciana.

It has one story worth telling a client. On 31 July 1944 Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, the legendary French pilot, took off from this airfield on a reconnaissance flight over France in a Lockheed P-38 Lightning and never came back.

The airport was in American hands at the time, used by the United States Army Air Forces Twelfth Air Force through 1944, with night fighter, photographic reconnaissance and bombardment units all based here at different points that year.
after:
The airport for Bastia and the north of Corsica, 17 km south south east of the city at Lucciana.

It has one story worth telling a client. On 31 July 1944 Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, the French pilot and author, took off from the wartime airfield at Borgo, in Corsica, on a reconnaissance flight over occupied France and never came back. The airport honours him with a memorial in front of its terminal, where it marks the anniversary.

claims.claim: on 31 July 1944 Saint-Exupery took off from the wartime airfield at Borgo on a reconnaissance flight over occupied France and never came back
claims.inAfter: On 31 July 1944 Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, the French pilot and author, took off from the wartime airfield at Borgo, in Corsica, on a reconnaissance flight over occupied France and never came back.
claims.note: Was 'took off from this airfield ... in a Lockheed P-38 Lightning'. The sources disagree on the airfield. English Wikipedia and the memorial at the terminal say this one; French Wikipedia says that, contrary to the memorial, he left from the field just to the north, called Bastia-Borgo, and his estate's own site says he took off from Borgo. The text follows the estate and French Wikipedia and makes no claim for Poretta. The aircraft for his last flight rests on English Wikipedia alone and is dropped.

claims.claim: took off from this airfield in a Lockheed P-38 Lightning
claims.wasBefore: On 31 July 1944 Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, the legendary French pilot, took off from this airfield on a reconnaissance flight over France in a Lockheed P-38 Lightning and never came back.
claims.why: Disputed: the memorial and English Wikipedia say this airfield; French Wikipedia and his estate's site say Borgo, the field just to the north. The aircraft for the last flight rests on English Wikipedia alone. Corrected (see above).

claims.claim: in American hands in 1944: the USAAF Twelfth Air Force, with night fighter, photographic reconnaissance and bombardment units
claims.wasBefore: The airport was in American hands at the time, used by the United States Army Air Forces Twelfth Air Force through 1944, with night fighter, photographic reconnaissance and bombardment units all based here at different points that year.
claims.why: Wikipedia alone (the English and French articles are one publisher). The 47th Bomb Group's own history says only that the group moved to Corsica on 11 July 1944, without naming the airfield, and the operator's history starts in 1945. The unit list may also run Poretta and Borgo together: the photographic reconnaissance squadrons it lists flew with Saint-Exupéry's group, which his estate places at Borgo.

claims.claim: fourteenth in France with about 1.5 million passengers in 2025; the runway lengthened in 1986; the first million in 2009
claims.why: Held back: new facts that replace nothing. The French airports' association ranks Bastia fourteenth in France with 1,532,265 passengers in 2025 (Eurostat 1,529,936); the operator's history has the runway built in 1954 and lengthened to 2,510 m in 1986, and the first million passengers in 2009.
